html:
On 5 December 1934 the parliament of Turkey gave women the right to vote and stand in national elections. Women had already won the local vote in 1930.

It was part of the reforms of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who presented equal rights for women as proof that the new republic was modern and Western. The Civil Code of 1926 had already given women equal rights in divorce and inheritance. Turkish feminists, such as those around Nezihe Muhiddin's Women's People's Party, had pressed for the vote since the 1920s, but the regime kept the reform in its own hands.

In the 1935 election 18 women entered parliament, about 4.5 percent of its members. Turkey acted ahead of France, which gave women the vote in 1944, and Italy, in 1946. Elections were then one-party, so the vote meant less than it seemed until multi-party politics came in 1946. Compare the much earlier women's suffrage in New Zealand.
sum: On 5 December 1934 the parliament of Turkey gave women the right to vote and stand in national elections. Women had already won the local vote in 1930.
